finding: On 1991-2026 history, more leverage always won: S&P 500 + SMA10 at 3x made 24.5%/yr (max DD -66%). But the forward simulation at today's valuations showed leverage does not raise the median.
decision: Leverage should follow the expected premium (Kelly: f = premium / variance). Try valuation-scaled leverage; widen leverage grids; lever the bond sleeve alone.
sources: Gayed & Bilello (2016) Leverage for the Long Run; Kelly (1956)

finding: Valuation-Kelly had the best TRAIN growth (13.8%/yr) but delevered through the 1991-2026 bull (test 14.9%). Expected wealth rises with leverage while median growth peaks near 2x (S&P+SMA10) or 2.5-3x (60/40+SMA10).
decision: Map the expected-value frontier so the leverage choice is explicit. Rank only strategies an ordinary margin account can hold (<=2x) separately from futures-only ones.
sources: Harvey et al. (2018) The Impact of Volatility Targeting; Ayres & Nalebuff, Lifecycle Investing

finding: Deployable champion: S&P 500 + SMA10 x2: 14.4%/yr since 1957, 18.1% on the untouched test period, max DD -47%, a 1987-style crash day costs -41%. Forward at CAPE 41: median 4.3%/yr (best of the frontier), mean wealth 1.83x in 10 years.
decision: Start forward paper accounts (deployable champion, research champion 60/40+SMA10 x3, 60/40 benchmark). Next: alternative trend signals under leverage, financing via leveraged ETFs (daily-reset decay), regime-specific leverage caps.

finding: Drawdown brake (test 21.2% vs 24.5% for plain 3x) and levered dual momentum (train picked 1x) lost. Seasonal leverage (3x Nov-Apr, 1x May-Oct) had the best TRAIN growth of any levered strategy (12.4%) and a smaller crash-day loss, but Sell-in-May largely vanished after its 2002 publication (t = 0.42 for 2003-2026). Valuation-scaled leverage to 3x: 15.7% test, max DD -42%.
decision: Champion unchanged. Seasonality goes on a watch list, not into the portfolio. Next: model leveraged-ETF daily-reset costs exactly with daily data, lifecycle de-leveraging, and combining the valuation and trend signals in one leverage rule.
sources: Bouman & Jacobsen (2002) The Halloween Indicator; Antonacci (2014) Dual Momentum Investing

finding: Recovery leverage (S&P 500 at 2x above its 10-month average, 3x while still >15% below its 36-month high) beat the 2x champion in training (11.6% vs 10.6%) and test (19.0% vs 18.1%), in all 12 depth/boost settings, with a higher forward median, higher average wealth and a lower chance of a 10-year loss. Variance management (Moreira-Muir) raised test growth only with more leverage and a lower forward median. Exp 16: a 2x/3x daily-reset S&P ETF matches cheap margin (+1.5%) and clearly beats retail margin (+5%), so up to 3x is reachable without a margin loan.
decision: New champion: recovery leverage (2x/3x via SSO/UPRO-style ETFs, cash otherwise). Added a 'deployable via ETFs' flag. Opened a forward paper account for it; the old 2x account continues as the margin champion. Next: when to exit faster in crashes (daily signal with a band), and a stock/bond version of recovery leverage.
sources: Moreira & Muir (2017) Volatility-Managed Portfolios; Poterba & Summers (1988); Exp 6, Exp 16

finding: Two changes to recovery leverage each beat it. (1) Exit only when BOTH the 10-month average and 12-month momentum turn down ('either' keeps you in): train 11.7% vs 11.6%, test 21.8% vs 19.0%, 125 vs 187 switches; pre-1957 roughly neutral (13.3% vs 13.0% in 1880-1929, 8.1% vs 8.4% in 1930-56). (2) Hold Treasuries instead of cash when out: train up to 13.2%. Combined (train-picked: 'either' + 2x bonds when out): train 13.6%, test 22.5%, 1957-2026 18.1%, forward median 6.8% vs 4.3%, average wealth 2.30x vs 1.89x, P(10-year loss) 14.5% vs 20.5%. COST: worst year -39% vs -30%, and 2022 -35% vs -10% (slower exit, then bonds fell with stocks). In the full-cost 5-year simulation it made 16.6%/yr vs 19.9% for the previous champion, max drawdown -41% vs -22%. A stock/bond recovery mix (0.8 stocks, 2x, 4x boost) tested 17.6%: lower growth, smaller crash-day loss (-33%).
decision: New champion by the loop rule (beats on test and forward median): recovery+ = 2x S&P (3x after >15% falls) while the S&P is above its 10-month average OR up over 12 months; 2x 7-10y Treasuries (UST) otherwise. The previous champion keeps its paper account for comparison. Watch item: stock-bond correlation regimes (2022, 1970s) are this rule's weak spot. Next: a bond-trend gate on the off-asset (hold bonds only when bonds are above their own 10-month average), then lifecycle de-leveraging.
sources: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012) Time Series Momentum; Alpha Architect (2016) What is the best risk-off asset for trend followers; CXO Advisory, Intrinsic momentum or SMA for avoiding crashes

finding: User: the algorithm must not depend on particular past years; it will trade unseen data. Audit: 219 variants have been tried against the same 1991-2026 test. A walk-forward simulation of the selection process itself (each year pick the best strategy on data known then) earned 14.9%/yr on 1991-2026 vs 22.5% for the hand-picked recovery+ champion. Most of that gap is hindsight. PSR that recovery+ has a higher Sharpe than the S&P: 0.86 (not significant). Eras never used for selection: recovery strategies made only ~8.7%/yr in 1930-1956 (≈ S&P 8.8%) because the post-crash 3x boost was caught in the false recoveries of 1930-32, while 2x/3x trend and valuation-scaled leverage made 12-19%. An equal-weight ensemble of three published effects (3x trend, valuation-scaled leverage ≤3x, recovery+) made 15.4% / 14.6% / 13.1% / 21.3% in the four eras (worst 13.1% vs 8.7% for recovery+). Forward 10-year: median 4.7%, average wealth 1.98x, P(loss) 17.5%. Full-cost 5 years: 19.9%/yr, max drawdown -26%, $398 trading costs.
decision: New champion: equal-weight ensemble (3x trend + valuation + recovery+), no fitted weights. New champion rule: rank by WORST era across 1880-1929, 1930-1956, 1957-1990 and 1991-2026; a challenger must not lose to the incumbent in any era (research.beats_everywhere); round-number, literature parameters only; the walk-forward selection return is reported as the honest estimate of what the loop itself can deliver. The only truly unseen data is the forward paper record from 2026-09. Data gap: the valuation sleeve needs monthly S&P earnings after 2023-06 (currently frozen at the last value).
sources: Bailey, Borwein, López de Prado & Zhu (2014) The Probability of Backtest Overfitting; Harvey & Liu (2015) Backtesting; Campbell & Shiller (1988); Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012); Poterba & Summers (1988)

finding: Two published whipsaw cures failed the worst-era rule. Growth-trend timing (obey the 10-month trend only when 12-month earnings growth, lagged 3 months, is negative): 2x gives 9.8% / 14.7% / 7.9% / 20.2% by era, max drawdown -75%. In 1973-74 earnings were still growing in nominal terms, so it stayed invested at 2x through the crash. This matches Newfound Research's mixed results outside the US. Multi-horizon trend (1/3/12-month TSMOM, Hurst-Ooi-Pedersen 2017) on one market at 3x: 10.4% / 16.4% / 9.5% / 20.2%, worse than the plain 10-month average in 3 of 4 eras; the 1-month signal adds noise. As ensemble sleeves, worst era 11.8% (growth-trend) and 12.3% (4 sleeves) vs the champion's 13.1%. Variants tried so far: 228. Walk-forward selection estimate unchanged: 14.3%/yr 1957-2026, 14.9% 1991-2026. Infrastructure: the real-time simulation stalled when FRED published the S&P close before the 10-year yield; the yield is now carried forward (a later change is booked when it becomes known).
decision: Champion unchanged (ensemble: 3x trend + valuation + recovery+, worst era 13.1%). Both ideas go to the explored list. Multi-horizon trend may still work across MANY markets (its published setting), which needs more data. Next: (1) diversify the trend sleeve across markets once data is reachable (FRED has gold, oil, dollar index and international indices); (2) a daily crash exit for the trend sleeve, tested on FRED daily S&P 2016-2026 plus the DJIA 2007-2016 file; (3) lifecycle / fixed-fraction de-leveraging.
sources: Philosophical Economics (2016) Growth and Trend; Newfound Research (2019) Global Growth-Trend Timing; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen (2017) A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing

finding: Exp 18, daily exits for the 3x trend sleeve (Gayed & Bilello 2016), daily 2007-2026 (DJIA to 2016 chained to the FRED S&P 500, T-bills from FRED, 5bp per switch). CAGR / max DD: monthly 10-month average 14.1% / -64%; daily 200-day 15.9% / -55%; daily 200-day with ±2% band 16.5% / -58%; monthly + daily emergency exit 11.7% / -56%; 3x buy & hold 16.4% / -94%. The banded daily rule beat the monthly rule in both halves (11.7% vs 11.1% in 2007-16, 21.6% vs 17.2% in 2017-26). It cut 2022 from -54% to -41%, but lost 8.6% in 2020 (sold in the March crash, re-entered late). The emergency exit was worst: it cut 2022 losses but whipsawed otherwise.
decision: No champion change. One daily era can't pass the worst-era rule, and daily data before 2007 is not available offline. The banded daily 200-day rule (3x) joins the real-time simulation as a NEW account, checked every trading day (live_sim gained a daily mode). If it keeps up in real time AND long daily history becomes available, test it as the ensemble's trend sleeve. Next: multi-market trend data (FRED NIKKEI225 since 1949, trade-weighted dollar, oil) and lifecycle de-leveraging.
sources: Gayed & Bilello (2016) Leverage for the Long Run (Dow Award paper); Exp 13 (banded 200-day)

finding: Exp 19, an out-of-sample MARKET: the Nikkei 225, 1950-2026 (FRED, month-ends, +1.5% dividends, US T-bill cash). No rule was designed on it, and it boomed to 1989 then fell -80% over 20 years. Same rules, nothing re-fitted. Buy & hold 1x: 10.3%/yr, max DD -75%. 10-month average 1x: 9.7%, -38%, roughly flat through the 1990-2012 bust. The 10-month average at 2x made 12.7% with a -77% drawdown; at 3x 12.9% with -94%. Recovery+ 11.1% with -97%. Buy & hold 3x was wiped out. A champion-like mix (valuation sleeve replaced by a neutral 1x trend sleeve, since Japan has no earnings data) lost up to -87%; with trend 2x and recovery 1-1.5x the worst fall was -61%. Lesson: the trend filter travels (halves drawdowns out of sample), but 3x leverage relies on the strong US drift. In a long sideways bust with whipsaws, the cost of being wrong at 3x compounds toward ruin. US eras for the lower-leverage ensemble (trend 2x, recovery 1-1.5x, 1x bonds when out): 12.5% / 12.9% / 11.7% / 15.8%, worst era 11.7% vs 13.1% for the champion; max DD -39% vs -53%; crash day -33% vs -47%; forward median 4.3% vs 4.7%, average wealth 1.72x vs 1.98x, P(10-year loss) 8% vs 18%.
decision: Champion unchanged under the current rule (US worst era). The trade-off (about 1.4 points a year of worst-era growth and lower expected wealth, for far better survival in a Japan-style market) is a risk-appetite choice for the owner, reported to them. The lower-leverage ensemble joins the real-time simulation as a NEW account. Protocol addition: champion candidates now also report a Japan stress test (Exp 19) for their testable sleeves. Next: international markets on FRED for more out-of-sample tests; a valuation proxy for Japan (dividend yield) if data can be found.
sources: FRED NIKKEI225; Gayed & Bilello (2016); Faber (2007); Exp 6 (US drift)
